Several hundred protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze ‌and looted shops in the centres of Milan, where more than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend.

In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have been blockading ports and highways to protest against the surge in fuel prices resulting from the US-Israel war on Iran.

France will offer interest-free loans of up to €50,000 to businesses affected by the riots and looting over the weekend, economy minister Roland Lescure said.

The scheme is expected to open on Friday, and should help traders with cash flow issues as they seek to get insurance payouts, the minister said, quoted by French media.

First court cases are also being progressed, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin confirming that 149 people have been put in provisional detention or imprisoned as part of ongoing trials. In a separate TV appearance on Monday evening, he said around 2,500 remained in custody for questioning, Reuters reported.

The number is expected to go up, as BFMTV reported that some 40 people are expected to appear in front of Parisian courts this afternoon.

In other news, it looks like France may have another problem coming its way, with heavy rainfall in the south of the country.

Parts of Corsica are now under a red alert for rain and flooding, with local flooding observed last night in several towns and village in the region. An all-time rainfall record broken in Salon-de-Provence, BFMTV reported.

The Gard department is on orange alert, with the coastal areas on a yellow alert.

Some flooding was also reported near Marseille.

As well as Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy will also meet the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre and the Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s new King Haakon during his visit to Oslo.

Jared Kushner is scheduled to attend digitally.

Ahead of the talks, Støre said that Zelenskyy has asked Norway and Finland to arrange a meeting as part of the ongoing diplomatic work, at a critical time for Ukraine. “Together with president Stubb, I am pleased to have such a meeting here in Oslo.”

Afterwards there will be a press conference with Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre and Zelenskyy has been invited for an audience at the palace.

The Ukrainian president is also due to meet with the Speaker and other members of the Norwegian parliament.

More than a month after the country went to the polls, Sweden is still without a government.

The Centre party’s Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist this week became the second party leader to be tasked with attempting to form a new coalition government (Europe Live, yesterday).

It comes after the Social Democrats’ Magdalena Andersson, whose party won the most votes in September’s general election, tried and failed to get the left leaning parties to come to agreement and lost a prime minister vote in parliament. The biggest stumbling block has been the Centre party’s refusal to go into government with the Left party.

This morning, however, after accepting the speaker’s task on Monday, Thand Ringqvist said she was not ruling out anything but that she wants to form a “middle government”. She has until Monday to report back to the speaker.

“I have booked in meetings with all party leaders but it will primarily be those who I have said can be part of a middle government,” she told broadcaster SVT. “I am not ruling out anything beforehand.”

Thand Ringqvist said she is not prepared to drop any of her so-called “redlines” when it comes to the Left party and the Sweden Democrats, both of whom she has ruled out going into government with. “That is why I am looking at the possibility of a middle alternative,” she said.

The Left party said that regardless of the outcome, they hope that Thand Ringqvist’s attempt will take parties out of the current deadlock.

Left party spokesperson Ida Gabrielsson said:

“Then it will be possible to sort out wether there are other alternatives. We want to have a government with S, V, C and MP (the Social Democrats, Left, Centre and Green parties). But the Centre party wants to have one in the middle. In which case it is good to find out whether it is possible or not.”

Social Democrat Mikael Damberg said his party will have “constructive discussions” with the Centre party if she wants to speak with them but that “you don’t get away from the maths of the Swedish parliament”.

The French parliament will look into formally opening an inquiry into the protests and violence seen in recent days, including the law enforcement measures used in response, after a political agreement was reached on this point, BFMTV reported.

No doubt we will hear more on this in due course.

I am also keeping an eye on events in Oslo, where US envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in the last hour for talks with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Norway and Finland.

Norway’s PM Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s Alexander Stubb will also join the discussion.

Televised images from Norwegian public broadcaster NRK showed Witkoff’s private jet landing just before noon at Oslo’s Gardermoen airport, AFP reported.

Ahead of the meeting with Witkoff, Zelenskyy spoke with US secretary of state Marco Rubio and said the pair had “a substantive conversation.”

“I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position. First, ballistic missile interceptors, which are needed to protect lives. Second, early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, which is vital. Third, the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored. Of course, all of this comes against the backdrop of our diplomatic efforts to end this horrific war and the constant killing of people.”

On his part, Rubio insisted that “nothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” AFP reported.

Meanwhile, the EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the bloc’s relationship with the UK is of “vital importance in the current geopolitical, security and economic context,” as he set out the bloc’s expectations ahead of next month’s EU-UK summit on 20 November.

Speaking at the European parliament in Strasbourg minutes after holding a phone call with UK’s Europe minister Hamish Falconer, he said the EU had three priorities for any talks with London.

Crucially, he wanted the two sides to fully implement the existing agreements, which include the protection of six million EU citizens resident in the UK and about a million UK nationals in the EU.

“We must ensure they can fully enjoy their rights now and in the future. That is why we continue to push for solutions on all matters affecting them,” he said.

He also said that “the work continues” on implementing the Windsor framework agreement, with its significance for Northern Ireland.

Šefčovič said the summit will also be a chance to look at sectoral issues, pointing to last year’s progress on fisheries, energy and Erasmus+.

“We aim to complete negotiations on a common sanitary and phytosanitary area, a linkage between our emissions trading systems and the creation of a youth experience scheme as a package for the summit,” he said.

He said there are also ongoing talks about the UK’s participation in the EU’s internal electricity market, and “an appropriate financial contribution from the UK towards the reducing economic, social and territorial disparities between regions in the union.”

The summit will also look at foreign policy issues, given the EU and the UK’s continued support for Ukraine.

He added that “given the geopolitical context, which is much changed since the withdrawal of the UK from the EU,” there is also scope for more work on supporting integrated value chains between the EU and the UK.

For a good summary of where we are when it comes to the French protests, you can catch up with Jon Henley’s commentary for The Latest.

“What we saw on Saturday was really an exceptional level of violence, even by French standards. In several towns and cities, there were attacks on those institutional targets. …

If this kind of violence continues, then that’s clearly a message that’s going to start appealing to more and more French voters.

Facing growing political pressure over the protests and riots, France’s PM Sébastien Lecornu will convene political parties for a meeting on Thursday, a member of his team said.

The conversation is also likely to touch upon the issue of policing, with critics saying the initial response to the protests was too heavy-handed.

He will also meet with trade unions on Wednesday.

The government has come under criticism from parties across the political spectrum, with far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen describing the unrest as a “wake-up call” that exposed a “profound crisis” of authority.

Meanwhile, president Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Gulf, the French presidency said.

With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tonnes per month, representing just over 10 percent of its consumption, the presidency added.

Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel supplies and bring down prices in France, after a weekend of violent protests sparked by soaring living costs.

A 40-year-old man was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of being involved in the arson attack that ravaged Limoges town hall over the weekend, French media reported.

The man is reportedly a “far-left activist” with a prior record that saw him placed on the security services’ watchlist, according to Le Figaro.

French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said that targeted curfews introduced in parts of Paris and other major cities “have contributed to calm overnight,” as he suggested more curfews could be introduced if needed today.

In a particular symbol of stepped up security measures, a helicopter flew over the French capital’s Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a powerful searchlight across the square, AFP said.

While some restrictions, such as those in Paris, initially applied only for the night from Monday to Tuesday, others, particularly in Bordeaux and Nice, were set to remain in force for several days, the agency noted.

Meanwhile, Italy’s government decided to dispatch 500 army troops to Milan after two days of unrest in the city, with shops in the city centre affected by riots and looting.

I will keep an eye on the latest from both France and Italy.

Elsewhere, the European parliament in Strasbourg will debate EU-UK relations this morning, and Nato’s Mark Rutte will host the Turkish foreign minister for talks. Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda is in Poland to discuss regional security.

I will bring you all the key news from across Europe here.

It’s Tuesday, 20 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
articles.excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challe...
articles.body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challenges.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that a combination of military attacks and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports “has dealt severe blows” to the country.

The admiral said the US had prevented at least $25bn in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze approximately $350m in cryptocurrency assets. This means the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are now unable to pay their soldiers and Iran-linked regional groups suffering from financial shortfalls.

“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said.

This is being portrayed as a victory for the US in its war with Iran, which so far has shown very few tangible victories for Washington.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at US-based intelligence and geopolitical risk advisory firm Horizon Engage, said Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen have suffered financially during the past few years.

“The national economies feeding the Hezbollah and Houthi movements are badly broken, so they continue to receive stipends and in-kind funding – in fuel products – from Iran,” Knights told Al Jazeera.

For decades, the IRGC Quds Force has supplied money, weapons, components, training and manufacturing expertise to regional allied groups. It has enabled partners at loggerheads with the US and Israel to assemble or produce a number of weapons locally, according to United Nations experts and US officials.

The axis groups also draw on businesses, including oil exports, as well as donations and local resources to fund their operations. Some Iraqi factions have been integrated into the official security forces and receive government funding through the Popular Mobilisation Forces.

Allied commercial networks in Iraq are selling Iranian commodities and distributing proceeds through intermediaries and exchange houses, the US Department of the Treasury has claimed.

This has put them in a better financial position than their “poorer cousins” in Hezbollah and the Houthis, Knights said, with some money allegedly flowing from Iraq towards Iran in recent years.

“Some Iraqi militiamen and government civil servants are indeed paid late at the same time that Iraqi militias send funding overseas to help Iran, the Houthis and Lebanese Hezbollah,” he told Al Jazeera.

The US Treasury alleged in September that Kataib Hezbollah, a prominent Tehran-backed Shia Muslim armed group in neighbouring Iraq, siphoned Iraqi resources to support Iran.

The Treasury also described substantial earlier transfers from the Quds Force to Hezbollah, depicting flows in both directions.

A report by the Reuters news agency earlier this month cited unnamed sources as saying Hezbollah received $200m from Iran in September. The US State Department rejected the report at the time, saying Hezbollah was “trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran”.

Iran’s economy has taken hit after hit in recent years due to war, domestic mismanagement and sanctions.

This has led to runaway inflation, low-paying jobs, a depreciating national currency and isolation from the global community for 90 million Iranians.

There appears to be little sign of the situation improving, with the World Bank reporting earlier this month a projected 7.7 percent contraction of the economy in the fiscal year 2026-27.

The authorities emphasise that does not affect their resolve. They have also challenged US Treasury assessments that economic pressure could result in losing control within months.

“Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier this month.

President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged on Sunday that military attacks and the maritime blockade had created substantial problems for the country. But he said his government was relying on domestic capacities to withstand the pressure.

He claimed consumption management had now removed the need for petrol imports that would otherwise cost $12bn, if US pressure allowed imports at all. The president promised to return revenues from recently increased fuel prices to households by modestly increasing their electronic food vouchers.

Knights said the Iranian authorities were “stuck in an aggressive cycle of escalation with the US government no matter what state Iran’s economy is in”.

“Trump is betting that being poorer will make Iran’s regime more flexible, but that has never been a good bet,” he said.

Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, said she expected Tehran to continue prioritising its regional allied groups despite the financial strains involved.

“Economic pressure is certainly constraining Iran’s military resources, but that does not mean it will fundamentally change the IRGC’s strategic calculations or force Tehran to surrender,” she told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Carmelo Anthony thinks Knicks are the 'team to beat' as long as they do this following NBA title win
articles.excerpt: New York Knicks legend Carmelo Anthony said a "target" is on the backs of his former team now that they are the current NBA champions entering a new year. He loved the playoff run last season, but kno...
articles.body_text:
New York Knicks legend Carmelo Anthony said a "target" is on the backs of his former team now that they are the current NBA champions entering a new year. He loved the playoff run last season, but knows what the Knicks must do to repeat.

Carmelo Anthony can’t wait for Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden, as he watches Jalen Brunson and the rest of the New York Knicks receive their long-awaited NBA title rings, and even better, watching a banner fly to the rafters for the first time in 53 years.

In fact, Anthony, who will be working the NBC Sports desk as part of their NBA crew, has to stop himself from prepping like he’s the one on the court wearing his No. 7 jersey again for the Knicks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"A game like tomorrow – opening night, ring night, banner night. Like right now, I’m preparing myself to get ready for the game like I’m about to go play," he told OutKick, while highlighting his partnership with DraftKings ahead of the 2026-27 NBA season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"And I have to pinch myself, like, ‘Yo bro, you ain’t getting back out there. You’re good on this side.’ Just the fact that I can still be in tuned to the game of basketball like that, and more importantly, to moments and still feel what those moments actually feel like.

Carmelo Anthony attends the New York Knicks 2026 championship parade and ceremony on June 18, 2026, at New York City Hall. (NBAE)

"I can imagine what will be going through those guys’ minds tomorrow, the adrenaline that will be pumping through them. Because winning one is a dream – we all dream of winning one. You don’t play this game without dreaming of winning a championship."

This past summer felt like a dream for millions of New Yorkers and others in the surrounding area who were all pulling for the Knicks to break their championship drought. It felt like destiny, from the OG Anunoby tip-in to win Game 4 against the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals, to the other key moments in their playoff run that Anthony and many other former Knicks had great seats for at The Garden.

But now, Anthony knows what comes with the title territory: everyone is hunting for the crown.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Defending it is a job," Anthony said. "So, nobody’s sneaking up on anybody anymore. That banner is going up there and the target goes on [the backs of the Knicks] instantly. Every team is going to circle the Knicks on the schedule, so that price of being champs in New York. You better embrace it and it’s going to be a fun ride."

The ride this past season was one Anthony didn’t want to get off. He admitted watching the team at first felt like he was a player all over again – until he realized he needed to just enjoy the moment like the rest of his peers and all Knicks fans hoping things would end with the Larry O’Brien Trophy being hoisted.

"I was putting myself into those moments and kind of thinking from a mental standpoint like, ‘What would I do here? What play?’ I was playing those games in my head, and then after a while I was like, ‘No, Melo, what are you doing? Just be a fan,’" he said. "So, I started to turn that part of my brain off and operating that way. To be a fan of basketball and the New York Knicks and of the players that were out there representing. It’s a beautiful thing, because as a former player, I love those moments. I live for those moments. The tip-in was like – ah! That was a moment! Jalen Brunson’s three was a moment. So, I understand what the Garden feels like in those moments, but that moment right there was special."

Jalen Brunson celebrates with the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy during the New York Knicks championship ticker-tape parade and victory rally in New York City. (Angelina Katsanis/Getty Images)

A new season brings new opportunity for not just the Knicks, but every NBA team hoping this will be their year. The Knicks have the crown, but teams like the Philadelphia 76ers, who will have LeBron James and Jaylen Brown suiting up for their first regular-season game with them in Madison Square Garden on Tuesday night, gunning for the title.

"When you know you have the crown, you’re not going to let anybody knock that crown off," Anthony said. "No matter what we gotta do, no matter how we gotta do it, no matter how hard it is to maintain this crown, we gotta do what we gotta do. And I think that’s the mentality coming into this season. Also, I think each individual player had to get better at something and get stronger in their weaknesses this offseason. If they did that, again, that’s the championship mindset.

"If they’re coming back like that, New York is the team to beat."

JOEL EMBIID REJECTS IDEA 76ERS STARS MUST 'TAKE A BACK SEAT' AS NBA REGULAR SEASON LOOMS

While Anthony is looking forward to what the Knicks do this season, he’s excited for his partnership with DraftKings and being a part of its campaign ahead of the season.

"We got a great campaign, man. Myself, Kevin Hart, Nick Jonas. We really came together, and I got to give a shoutout to DraftKings and that creative team for putting that concept together," he said. "The beauty in that is the fact that we can have more fun with DraftKings because it’s in all 50 states now, which is major. I just love the fact that more people are involved, and more people can have fun with the game of basketball in this sense, and just sports in general. I love that."

Carmelo Anthony and John Starks ride on a float during the New York Knicks championship ticker-tape parade and victory rally on June 18, 2026, in New York City. The Knicks defeated the San Antonio Spurs in five games to win their first NBA Championship in 53 years. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Anthony called it a "beautiful thing" being able to work alongside Hart and Jonas for the campaign, which he is excited for fans to see.

With DraftKings available in all 50 states, the campaign revolves around Hart and Jonas traveling throughout the country, where car troubles can happen. As the tow truck figures out their situation, Anthony is waiting with his own car problems in the clip as he tries to get the word out about DraftKings.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Zelensky prepares for Oslo talks with US envoys as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
articles.excerpt:
Volodymyr Zelensky arrived at Oslo airport on Tuesday ahead of the talks with Witkoff

US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the...
articles.body_text:
Volodymyr Zelensky arrived at Oslo airport on Tuesday ahead of the talks with Witkoff

US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".

Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.

He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.

"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.

Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.

The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.

Steve Witkoff was due to hold talks in Oslo in person while Jared Kushner was taking part remotely

Witkoff is expected to be joined by video-link by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, and by several European representatives, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and officials from the UK, Poland, France and Germany, as well as the EU and Nato.

It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".

Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and afterwards the US president announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Trump's deal with the Russian leader coincided with Witkoff and Kushner's last meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami, and Zelensky reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present for Putin".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have reached record highs at the pump since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".

He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."

articles.title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
articles.excerpt:
France saw some of the worst disorder in its modern history on Saturday, with the violence in Marseille among the most serious

Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend...
articles.body_text:
France saw some of the worst disorder in its modern history on Saturday, with the violence in Marseille among the most serious

Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.

France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.

A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.

So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.

But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.

Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence

Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media

It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.

Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors is expected to be announced for some parts of the city from Tuesday.

Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.

18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away.

"It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.

Maryam (R) joined the protests on Saturday, which began in September over poor school conditions before escalating to cover broader issues such as the cost of living

Maryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.

She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen.

"It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began.

"But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact.

For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers.

"It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."

Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.

Police union representative Arnaud Blaise said police had eventually run out of ammunition

Blaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc.

"The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."

I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses.

"That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured.

"Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."

'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight

Watch: Mass vandalism on Marseille streets

Watch: Shops looted and restaurants gutted in Paris riots

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.

He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan.

Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen.

"Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.

He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics.

"If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."

He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."

Chantal Bellanger said she was worried for young people rioting out of anger and despair

While the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.

At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time".

"We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."

She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair.

"It tugs at your heartstrings," she said.

"To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."

Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

articles.title: France PM promises more curfews as authorities seek to regain control
articles.excerpt: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said new curfews will be imposed where necessary in parts of the country, as authorities sought to restore order after weekend demonstrations over the cost ...
articles.body_text:
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said new curfews will be imposed where necessary in parts of the country, as authorities sought to restore order after weekend demonstrations over the cost of living and issues in the education system descended into riots.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Lecornu said local authorities would coordinate with mayors to decide whether to impose curfews in their respective prefectures.

More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday for demonstrations that brought together students demanding better education conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living. The protests descended into looting and arson in numerous locations, with more than 2,500 people arrested.

Monday night passed without any major incidents across France, police have confirmed.

The government is due to hold a series of meetings as it intensifies efforts to contain the unrest, which followed weeks of student protests over education standards.

French Digital Minister Anne Le Henanff is due to meet social media bosses on Tuesday to discuss the protests. In a post on X on Monday, Henanff said goods looted over the weekend were being sold online and called on platforms to remove such listings.

Demonstrators have called for further protests this Saturday, but France’s main trade unions have not backed the call, with union officials due to meet Lecornu on Wednesday. On Thursday, Lecornu will hold talks with political parties about the protests, which come before presidential elections due to take place in April and May next year.

Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, currently leads the polls. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who leads La France Insoumise, is currently in second place. President Emmanuel Macron cannot stand because of France’s two-term limit.

Le Pen and Melenchon have both been accused of exploiting the protests before next year’s vote.

Alice Cohen-Morzadec, a spokesperson for the French Student Union, told Al Jazeera that the demonstrations were an “outburst” of anger in response to Macron’s policies, which she said had “destroyed” students’ living conditions.

“One student out of two cannot eat properly. One student out of three doesn’t have a permanent house to live in. We cannot study in these conditions,” Cohen-Morzadec said.

articles.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
articles.excerpt: A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, ...
articles.body_text:
A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site.

Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE.

LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence.

ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported.

So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out:

A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring.

Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported.

In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite.

ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies.

ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres.

Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios.

Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away.

A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.

In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite.

In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military.

Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.”

However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference.

“It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.”

Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.”

This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”.

Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this.

Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”.

It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres.

Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground.

Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

For Hilborne, the choice of target “is starting to indicate that Russia does not distinguish between commercial and military satellites as potential targets”.

That matters because militaries, including Ukraine’s, increasingly rely on commercial satellites for communications and imagery.

In October 2022, a senior Russian foreign ministry official told the United Nations that “quasi-civilian infrastructure may be a legitimate target for a retaliatory strike”.

Juliana Suess, a space security researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, said Russia may be calculating that reactions will be less severe if it shadows a commercial satellite rather than a sovereign one, especially one not belonging to the US.

ICEYE-X36 is owned by ICEYE’s US subsidiary and registered as a US satellite, Hilborne noted, adding, “this creates a complex problem”.

The distance matters too. A gap of less than 5km may sound far, Suess said, but “it’s essentially a hop and a skip in space”.

“It’s incredibly close and could potentially enable Russia to conduct nefarious activity, including intercepting data from the satellite or disrupting its service – temporarily via signal jamming, for example,” she added.

“A kinetic attack would also be possible but seems less likely at this point in time, in part because this would be an unprecedented measure taken against a satellite”, she explained.

“It is sending a message that these platforms could be held under threat,” Hilborne said, adding that it also represents an escalation, suggesting Russia might be willing to attack, since any satellite could be used as a weapon simply by crashing it into another.

Suess added: “I think regardless of whether we see further manoeuvring or consequences, the political goal of intimidation should not be underestimated”.

“The manoeuvre is also a message that space assets cannot be considered wholly safe or removed from the war in Ukraine”, she said.

She pointed to November 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites with a missile, an event referred to in the European Union’s 2023 space strategy.

“We have long known what Russia is capable of in terms of disrupting or even destroying space assets. This manoeuvre is also a reminder of those previously demonstrated capabilities,” she said.

Moscow calls such spacecraft “inspector satellites”, and in 2020 described such manoeuvres as common practice “by many countries”, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.

Hilborne described the approach as “another example of activity that sits below the threshold of conflict”.

An outright attack on ICEYE-X36 looks unlikely for now, Hilborne said.

“With the current balance in the conflict, and this being an American-registered satellite, it would seem unlikely that Russia would actually attack the satellite, as the response would be unpredictable”, he said.

An attack could also create a large amount of space debris, which would be a problem for everyone, he added, warning that “it’s hard to second-guess where Russia draws the line”.

Ukraine’s access to satellites has come under pressure before, at times from its own allies.

In March 2025, as Washington paused intelligence sharing with Kyiv, the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency “temporarily suspended” Ukraine’s access to the main portal for US government-purchased commercial imagery.

If ICEYE-X36 were disrupted, Ukraine would not necessarily go blind, Suess said, because the ICEYE constellation has more than one satellite, and sovereign radar satellites, such as Germany’s, could also provide data.

But speed is the issue. According to ICEYE, the expanded access agreed this year meant faster access, Suess explained.

“The question is whether a similarly fast transfer of data could be enabled with a new provider, whether commercial or sovereign in nature,” she said.

Now, Ukraine faces another squeeze. Last week, the order to limit Starshield – the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service – for Ukraine came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.

On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starshield is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but that Kyiv’s request to use it for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

articles.title: Senate Republicans might survive the blue thunderstorm. Uh, I think.
articles.excerpt:
Kansas voters Felita Kahrs and William Six join 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the tight Senate race between GOP candidate Roger Marshall and Democrat candidate Adam Hamilton.

With everyone and his broth...
articles.body_text:
Kansas voters Felita Kahrs and William Six join 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the tight Senate race between GOP candidate Roger Marshall and Democrat candidate Adam Hamilton.

With everyone and his brother predicting that a blue tsunami will wash over the Senate as well as the House, I want to write something contrarian.

This way, if the Republicans do hang on to the Senate, I’ll get credit for defying the conventional wisdom. And if they don’t, I won’t get kicked out of the punditocracy – folks will just say well, he put a lot of caveats in there.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

The truth is, I don’t know who is going to capture the upper chamber, and neither do you.

And neither do all the pontificators and speculators online or on the air.

A view of the US Senate office as the US Capitol Police (USCP).  (Celal Gunes/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

I do know the GOP is pouring tens of millions into contests they might otherwise lose, giving their people – even scandal-scarred Ken Paxton – a huge advantage on the airwaves in the final two weeks. But money doesn’t always move voters once they’ve made up their minds in this era of early voting.

Is Maine’s Susan Collins liked enough to hang one more time against aggressive Troy Jackson (and thankfully not weirdo Graham Platner), when Donald Trump shouts every day ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot’?" We got it, Mr. President.

Josh Turek is an Iowa legislator and also a wheelchair basketball player who suffers from spina bifida. His GOP opponent, Rep. Ashley Hinton, says she doesn’t want "endless wars" but welcomes a Trump visit.

She’s talked about such issues as open borders and transgender surgery. Turek has focused on the Iran war and soaring health premiums because Congress failed to amend the Affordable Care Act.

In nearby Kansas, where Trump campaigned yesterday, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the founder of a Methodist mega-church, which would seem like a big plus in that conservative state, but some Dems are turned off by the religious aspect. Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an obstetrician who served in the Army Reserves, was hurt by a New York Times report on him suing patients who were behind on their bills.

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

By the way, did you ever think you’d see the day when the Republicans just gave up on North Carolina and steered their money elsewhere (conceding the win to former Gov. Roy Cooper)?

PRESIDENT TRUMP HEADS TO KANSAS TO CAMPAIGN FOR SEN ROGER MARSHALL

Many of these races have 1-or-2 point "leads," which is within the margin of error, and polling is often inaccurate in an off-year election.

The GOP is playing defense in ruby-red states–Trump in Kansas?—which is why Democrats are increasingly confident this is their big year.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

And, in the famous Tip O’Neill saying, all politics is local.

There may be a mega-church guy or a man in a wheelchair or ex-Alaska congresswoman Mary Peltola, a former tribal judge who’s for "Fish, Family, Freedom," but who former staffers say they heard using awful slurs.

How on earth do you handicap races with so many toss-ups?

Of course, Republicans want to make the country believe that all Dems are like Michigan socialist Abdul el-Sayed, who, when asked whether he’d provide military aid if Israel was under attack, says he would rather spend the money at home.

I still think the Democrats will need to have Vegas luck to win enough Senate races to take control. They also have to defend their own turf. But (escape hatch here) I’m not saying it couldn’t happen.

Howard Kurtz is a media and political analyst and the former host of FOX News Channel's MediaBuzz. Based in Washington, D.C., he joined the network in 2013 and regularly appears on Special Report with Bret Baier and The Story with Martha MacCallum among other programs.

articles.title: Alberta voters reject separation from Canada, early results show
articles.excerpt: Alberta residents have voted to remain ⁠part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he ‌attempts to unify the country a...
articles.body_text:
Alberta residents have voted to remain ⁠part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he ‌attempts to unify the country amid an ongoing trade war with the United States.

With more than one million votes counted, about 76 percent supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23 percent who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation, early results showed on Tuesday.

The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path towards a future vote on separation from Canada.

articles.title: French cities calm overnight after curfews imposed to quell violence, PM says
articles.excerpt:
Clean up begins after French riots but police remain

Targeted curfews across France contributed to a quiet night following a weekend of riots and looting across the country, the Prime Minister Sébast...
articles.body_text:
Clean up begins after French riots but police remain

Targeted curfews across France contributed to a quiet night following a weekend of riots and looting across the country, the Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said.

Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they are necessary.

Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.

The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night

Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.

He had been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.

In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters

articles.title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
articles.excerpt:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was p...
articles.body_text:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.

That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.

“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”

It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.

The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.

The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.

R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.

After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.

Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)

“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”

But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.

“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”

With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.

During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.

Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.

“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.

R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.

Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)

R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.

“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.

Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.

It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”

Culture | Two Indian films won awards at the Busan international film festival. Birds in the Dark by Shashank Walia was awarded the Songwon Vision audience prize and Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi won the HyLife Vision as well as the Taipei Film Commission award.

Politics | The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October for his second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.

Imran Khan | Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khan appeared at a Mumbai protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.

A recommendation from someone with great taste

With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.

“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”

Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.

Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.

“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.

The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7%
articles.excerpt:
ONS data shows rate down from 4.9% but number of job vacancies continues to shrink

Unemployment in the UK fell unexpectedly in the three months to August, to 4.7% from 4.9%.

The Office for National ...
articles.body_text:
ONS data shows rate down from 4.9% but number of job vacancies continues to shrink

Unemployment in the UK fell unexpectedly in the three months to August, to 4.7% from 4.9%.

The Office for National Statistics figures, which provide a backdrop to the budget on 28 October, also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3m.

However, the number of job vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic.

Economists had expected the unemployment rate to rise to 5%.

Average wage growth, including bonuses, has fallen to 3.7% from 3.9%. Stripping out bonuses, average pay growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6%.

Average pay growth remains above the 3.1% headline rate of inflation, which is of concern to Bank of England interest rate setters, who fear higher-than-expected inflation will translate into higher wage awards, fuelling future prices rises recorded by the consumer prices index (CPI).

articles.title: A young life ‘dominated by gambling’: Victorian coroner delivers stinging findings on death of 22-year-old
articles.excerpt:
Online betting was the ‘direct and paramount’ cause behind Kyle Hudson’s decision to take his own life, inquest finds

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Kyle Hudson was “a y...
articles.body_text:
Online betting was the ‘direct and paramount’ cause behind Kyle Hudson’s decision to take his own life, inquest finds

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Kyle Hudson was “a young man brimming with promise”, with a loving and supportive partner, family and friends, and prospects.

“It was a near ideal picture – except for the grip that online sports betting had upon him,” the Victorian coroner Paul Lawrie said on Tuesday.

Lawrie, delivering his findings into the 22-year-old Werribee man’s death, said Hudson’s online gambling was “the direct and paramount causative factor underlying his decision to take his own life” on 6 July 2021.

“Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling,” Lawrie said.

The inquest, held in May, examined the immediate circumstances and likely contributing factors to Hudson’s death, his personal and financial history, his online gambling history, and whether some of Australia’s largest betting companies accurately assessed Hudson’s risk of gambling-related harm in the years prior to his death.

Hudson opened his first online gambling account with Sportsbet on his 18th birthday in 2017. He gambled $895,733 through Sportsbet and other online betting platforms run by Entain and Bet365 over four years, with the last bets placed hours before he took his own life.

Hudson’s online betting was also the “indisputable” direct cause of the breakdown of his relationship with his longtime girlfriend, Ashley Baker, in the days immediately preceding his suicide, the coroner found.

“Her account of the decline of their relationship makes clear the corrosive effect of Kyle’s gambling,” Lawrie said.

The coroner, at times becoming emotional, was scathing of an “extraordinary” submission made by Sportsbet, with whom 85% of Hudson’s gambling had occurred.

Sportsbet had argued that the court had not seen sufficient evidence to conclude Hudson had been suffering from gambling harm.

“It is chilling that this is Sportsbet’s view,” Lawrie said.

Hudson made bets on 110 of the 187 days in the last six months of his life, averaging 9.2 bets for each betting day. Over the four years he gambled with Sportsbet, Hudson had triggered behavioural alerts within the company’s systems on 37 occasions – once every six weeks on average, with the first occurring within two months of his 18th birthday.

The betting companies told the inquest they believed at the time that Hudson was “betting within limits” and that he never met their highest risk threshold, though representatives from Entain and Bet365 acknowledged in evidence that, with all the facts in view, Hudson appeared to have been suffering from gambling harm.

“Sportsbet maintains that Kyle was not suffering from problem gambling,” Lawrie said.

“I do not accept this proposition. The analysis of Kyle’s betting activity detailed above presents a startling picture of a young man whose life after age 18 was dominated by online gambling.”

Hudson had engaged in problem gambling throughout much of the four years, and “as a consequence, he suffered significant gambling harm, which increased as time progressed”, the coroner found.

“The impact went far beyond the money Kyle lost. Online gambling had taken over so much of his life. This is made crystal clear in the astonishing measurements of his betting activity,” he said.

Hudson sustained an overall net loss of more than $47,000 through gambling, a forensic accounting analysis had shown, but the coroner found it would have been difficult for Hudson to have known precisely how high his tally of losses was. The coroner recommended the federal government change the consumer framework to require online betting companies to prominently display customers’ net financial position over time in their accounts.

Hudson redeemed 489 inducements over the four years he was gambling. There could be “little doubt” that the promotions and inducements Hudson received over the years “catalysed Kyle’s betting behaviour” and had a “contrary and corrosive impact” on the effect of any of the gambling companies’ safer gambling efforts, the coroner said.

Gambling companies provided the details of their advertising budgets to the court confidentially, under a claim of commercial sensitivity. Lawrie did not reveal those figures, but on Tuesday described them as “a level of expenditure on gambling advertising in Australia that is arresting”.

“It is close to impossible to move through the modern world without being exposed to [gambling] advertising,” Lawrie said.

“Kyle did not decide out of nowhere to open his first betting account on his 18th birthday … There can be little doubt that Kyle began his online gambling as soon as he could because he was primed by the phenomenon that was swirling about him before he turned 18.”

He recommended the Australian government consider further restrictions, including prohibitions on advertising for online gambling, and establish a national online gambling regulator to oversee licensing, safety, gambling harm interventions and data collection.

He also recommended the government establish and fund an independent “data vault”, which he said had been introduced in various European countries, and allowed for better regulation of online gambling companies. This vault would hold standardised gambling data, which gambling companies would be compelled to provide, and mechanisms to allow for thorough independent research on gambling harm and gambling safety.

There were “critical and obvious deficiencies” in the current system of monitoring and intervention for online gambling harm, which lay mainly with companies themselves, and relied on partial data and, sometimes, verbal assurances from a customer that they were betting safely, the coroner said.

Hudson’s case “should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies”, Lawrie said.

articles.title: ‘Lack of curiosity’ about family’s religious beliefs was ‘missed opportunity’ to save eight-year-old, inquest hears
articles.excerpt:
Coroner says she’s considering adopting recommendations from Victoria’s cults inquiry as investigation into Elizabeth Struh’s death continues

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podca...
articles.body_text:
Coroner says she’s considering adopting recommendations from Victoria’s cults inquiry as investigation into Elizabeth Struh’s death continues

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The coroner investigating the death of Elizabeth Struhs is considering adopting recommendations from Victoria’s cults inquiry, warning a “lack of curiosity” about her family’s religious beliefs was a “missed opportunity”.

Elizabeth, an eight-year-old, died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis after her father ceased providing insulin to treat type 1 diabetes.

The rest of her family and other members of a religious sect known as the “saints” subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and didn’t believe in seeking medical treatment for illnesses. They sat around singing and praying for her resurrection after her death.

The young girl came to the attention of multiple government departments after a 2019 hospitalisation for diabetic ketoacidosis. She was extremely unwell because her parents delayed seeking medical help for her, and were both convicted of child neglect.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is sitting for the seventh day of an inquest into Elizabeth’s death.

Kirkegaard has previously heard that Elizabeth’s mother, Kerrie Struhs, had repeatedly told police, healthcare workers, teachers, parole officers and child safety workers about her views and that she would do the same thing again.

They were also discussed at a formal interagency case management meeting by the suspected child abuse and neglect team.

But the coroner said none of them seemed curious about Kerrie’s “really quite extraordinary beliefs”.

“What’s striking in the evidence that’s available to me, is an acceptance of this mother’s beliefs without any curiosity about why she held them,” she said.

“And the missed opportunity that flows from that lack of curiosity to have identified the broader influences for the children within this family.”

Kirkegaard has asked several witnesses about their level of curiosity about Kerrie’s beliefs. Many have said they weren’t curious at all, or they were only curious about the degree to which they created a risk to her daughter, not their origins.

One child safety officer who said she was curious told the court: “I don’t recall doing anything specific” in response to her interest.

She conceded it was a missed opportunity to protect Elizabeth.

Kerrie’s church group was ultimately deemed a source of support for her by child safety.

All 14 adult members of the Saints were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year.

On Tuesday, Kirkegaard heard from three senior figures in the Queensland police, Queensland Department of Education and the health department.

The coroner has asked all of them about Victoria’s inquiry into the recruitment methods and impacts of cults and organised fringe groups, in an apparent effort to gauge whether similar recommendations might be appropriate in response to the death of Elizabeth.

Victoria’s inquiry recommended creating a new offence akin to the domestic violence offence of coercive control to apply in the context of an organised group, such as a cult, among others.

A senior police officer told her that Victoria’s findings would be relevant to Queensland but could not be automatically adopted without an assessment of Queensland’s law.

“A key concern has to be religious friends and making sure that we’re not targeting religious groups based on their ideologies,” he said.

He told the coroner that it was a “complex area” to define.

“We have parents who believe in traditional medicine and they want to use alternative medicine. When does that pose a risk to a child that reaches a threshold for statutory investigation?”

Queensland police have only recently created a reporting mechanism or crime class reflecting cult-related offending, he said, but created one in June 2026 identifying “ideology of concern”.

“The flag was created to expand upon the existing ‘sovereign citizen’ flag within QPrime to identify persons displaying other types of ideologies of concern including religious, racist and anti-government ideologies,” the officer told the court.

No witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

articles.title: US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms
articles.excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to  end Russia’s war.

“Zelenskyy is a man that should h...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to  end Russia’s war.

“Zelenskyy is a man that should have had settled this war a long time ago. If he would’ve listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Monday. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.”

The US president has been verbally swiping at his Ukrainian counterpart for several days as a rift between the leaders deepens.

On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Zelenskyy does not want to end the war. Earlier this month, he called for him to be replaced as president, and labelled him a “warmonger” over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Trump has also defended sanctions waivers for Russia, saying in the same Truth Social post that he wants to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

Zelenskyy said the decision “will hurt Ukraine” and strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

Trump also announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.

The decision has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and US officials, who say it rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told US senators at a meeting on Monday that decisions taken by the Trump administration “are hard to explain between friends”.

He said arms shipments had been delayed and intelligence sharing restricted.

“We also know that … the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) programme,” he said.

To his knowledge, he added, one missile package was waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval.

In remarks posted in a video on Telegram, Zelenskyy said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of Russian attacks generally provided by its partners.

Last week, Zelenskyy suggested a disruption of Starlink services in Ukraine was “deliberate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the claim.

The sparring comes as Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, the Reuters news agency reported, citing three people familiar with the matter.

Two of the sources said they expected Zelenskyy to attend the meetings.

The Oslo discussions are expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland – the European Union, and NATO.
