articles.title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists
articles.excerpt:
Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold second binding independence vote

Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has ex...
articles.body_text:
Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold second binding independence vote

Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.

On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second binding independence referendum.

A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.

Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, a blaze tore through the CFB Wainwright and into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.

The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.

Nevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.

Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.

The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.

Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.

Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

Carney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.

Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.

“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.

Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

The movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently published the Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.

Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.

Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.

“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”

Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.

“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”

“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”

Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.

One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.

In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.

“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.

“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”

In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operatives and staff at the US state department. Among items allegedly discussed were how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.

No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.

The president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”

Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”

He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including an unexplained halt to talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.

“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”

articles.title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian town as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
articles.excerpt:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the fastest-warming places in the world

Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one...
articles.body_text:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the fastest-warming places in the world

Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.

Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.

Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade.

Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining town.

“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.

When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.”

The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”.

Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.

Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.

Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.

Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience.

The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around. Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.

“In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources.”

Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.

“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the Arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

articles.title: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
articles.excerpt:
Letter from 150 scientists, MPs and activists calls for action to protect lower-income and minority-ethnic communities

The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 1...
articles.body_text:
Letter from 150 scientists, MPs and activists calls for action to protect lower-income and minority-ethnic communities

The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 150 scientists, MPs and activists have urged.

Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that across England, lower-income areas have persistently higher levels of air pollution than wealthier areas.

The same research found that minority-ethnic populations were exposed to air pollution levels that were about 6% higher than those experienced by white populations.

In a letter signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including the climate activist Greta Thunberg, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been urged to hold a national inquiry into the impacts of air pollution on these groups.

Exposure to air pollution is linked to heart disease, strokes, cancer, asthma and effects on lung development in children. Despite this, the letter says, the UK does not have a dedicated mechanism to address the health inequalities.

Air pollution can come from a wide range of sources, from wood-burning stoves to industrial fossil fuel burning. But the leading threat to clean air is posed by traffic emissions, with petrol and diesel vehicles emitting a variety of toxic pollutants. Measures such as London’s ultra-low emission zone have had a significant impact on improving air quality, with children’s lungs found to have grown bigger and stronger as a result of the policy.

While there has been marked progress in reducing air pollution in cities like London, new government data shows that in 2025, parts of London, Glasgow and Bristol still had illegal levels of air pollution.

Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the mother of a nine-year-old girl who became the first person in the UK to have air pollution cited on their death certificate, said a “failure of inaction by all the main political parties over so many years, has meant the UK population is exposed to illegal levels of emissions”.

This warning comes as new data, obtained through freedom of information requests by the campaign group Mums for Lungs, shows that in 11 English cities and areas, including London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham, more than 200,000 children were taken to hospital with breathing difficulties in 2025. The research found that younger children were the most affected, with more than 120,000 babies and toddlers admitted to A&E or hospital.

Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs are still developing and they breathe more air relative to their body size than adults.

In the city of Manchester, there has been a stark increase in admissions of babies and toddlers, rising from 653 in 2023 to 1,072 in 2025.

Mums for Lungs said the decision in 2023 by Burnham, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, to scrap plans for a clean air zone raised important questions about whether sufficient action was being taken to drive down pollution levels.

Jemima Hartshorn, the campaign group’s founder, declared the situation an “air pollution emergency”.

“Behind every number is a child who is struggling to breathe and a family looking for help. We cannot keep treating dirty air as inevitable or acceptable,” she said.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “Air quality continues to improve over the longer term and while most air quality standards are being met, more action is needed to protect communities.

“Our ambitious new targets will cut harmful particle exposure by nearly a third by 2030. Working together with local authorities will keep driving progress through clean air plans and robust monitoring.”

articles.title: Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: NHS Alliance’s acute care director says centralisation of services ‘inevitable’ to ensure safe care

Why are some NHS maternity units facing closure?

Up to 20 maternity units in England wi...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: NHS Alliance’s acute care director says centralisation of services ‘inevitable’ to ensure safe care

Why are some NHS maternity units facing closure?

Up to 20 maternity units in England will have to shut to ensure mothers and babies receive safe care amid shortages of doctors and rising caesarean section rates, an NHS leader has warned.

Matthew Hopkins, the NHS Alliance’s director for acute care, said centralising childbirth services into fewer hospitals was “inevitable” and the “right thing”, but would lead to a political backlash against unpopular changes.

Ministers must “grasp the nettle” that as many as 20 of England’s 155 NHS units that are led by consultant obstetricians will need to shut or change their role, he added.

Hopkins urged ministers and MPs to show “courage” by backing major changes to where maternity services are located, even though reconfigurations will lead to mothers-to-be in affected areas being forced to travel further to have their babies.

Smaller maternity units that deliver only 1,500 to 2,000 babies a year are becoming increasingly unsustainable because of a widespread lack of obstetricians and a sharp rise in recent years in the number of women having either a planned or emergency caesarean section, he added.

Many of the units most at risk are in rural or coastal areas, where staffing is particularly challenging, he told the Guardian. “We are calling for a thorough appraisal of maternity services and where they need to be located because the current configuration is not fit for purpose,” Hopkins said.

“Difficult decisions lie ahead, consolidating maternity services to support safer, more sustainable care.

“If politicians … are keen to see safe maternity services in their area, it is going to need courage to grasp the nettle that needs to be grasped in order to improve maternity services.”

Consolidation of care at fewer sites was “inevitable” and represented “doing the right thing … the safe thing for patients”, he said. Maternity units with too few doctors could not provide the level of service needed to ensure safety, he stressed.

Hospital bosses fear that the government’s maternity taskforce, which is due to publish a report on improving childbirth care before Christmas, “will be tokenistic and won’t deal with the real strategic issues that underpin the problems” if it does not set out clearly how the NHS should accommodate the rise in caesarean sections, which require units to have more staff and more operating theatres, Hopkins added.

But his comments provoked an immediate outcry, with obstetricians and midwives insisting that maternity care should remain a service the NHS provides near people’s homes. “Women and families rely on local maternity units to be there when they need them, and we must ensure there are high-quality services close to home,” said Hannah Leonard, the chief policy officer of the Royal College of Midwives.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, said: “There are other solutions to our workforce challenges that are far safer than closing maternity units, and these should be explored.”

Hopkins’s comments came as the Royal Devon university healthcare NHS foundation trust was expected to decide this week if the maternity unit at North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple, which shut temporarily in August due to understaffing, now has enough doctors to allow it to safely reopen.

Andy Burnham, in his first appearance at prime minister’s questions on 2 September, admitted that maternity services across the whole UK were facing “structural issues”. Burnham told the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, it was “not acceptable” for expectant mothers from north Devon to have to give birth in Exeter, which is 43 miles – and a 70-minute car journey – from Barnstaple.

An estimated 194 women have had their child in Exeter because of the closure.

The maternity unit at Yeovil hospital in Somerset reopened earlier this year after being shut for almost 12 months because it had too few staff. The maternity unit at Daisy Hill hospital in Newry, in Northern Ireland, was last month earmarked for closure for the same reason. Strenuous efforts by NHS bosses to recruit obstetricians from Ireland, the UK and internationally to work there failed.

Closing rural and coastal units would put mothers and babies in danger, said Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrat health spokesperson. “Forcing women in labour to travel an hour or more to the nearest hospital is unsafe, unacceptable, and leaves local communities abandoned,” she said, adding that ministers must not allow maternity services in rural and coastal areas to be “shuttered”.

Hopkins – who has run four hospital trusts – is not the first senior figure to argue for major reconfiguration of maternity services to improve the quality and safety of care.

Marian Knight, a professor of maternal and child population health at the University of Oxford, who investigates maternal deaths as part of the MBRRACE-UK research programme, told the Health Service Journal last month that the NHS should consider “consolidation into fewer, bigger [maternity] units to help medical teams manage the surge in C-sections”. They rose from 33% of births in England in 2020 to 45% last year.

Some women who died during childbirth between 2022 and 2024 did so because their caesarean section was delayed or postponed because an obstetric surgeon or operating theatre was not available, the most recent MBRRACE-UK report found. “It was not clear if the safety of services is maintained in light of [the] increased demand [for caesarean sections]”, it said.

Urging immediate action on centralisation of care, Hopkins added: “If this C-section rate becomes 55% or 65%, [that] inevitably will force reactive actions being taken. In our view, [and] Marian’s view, we need to grasp the nettle and get ahead of what could be really difficult conditions for mums, babies and staff if this rate of increase in C-sections continues to rise.”

In her government-commissioned review of maternity care in June, Valerie Amos revealed that senior figures in the field had told her that key challenges to improving care included “poor infrastructure, with, at times, unsafe and unacceptable estates … and too little (political) backing for difficult reconfiguration decisions.”

The Department of Health and Social Care did not comment directly on possible maternity unit closures.

But a spokesperson said: “Every woman deserves safe maternity care, and the Secretary of State has made this issue a personal priority. Through the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, that she is chairing, this government will deliver the reforms needed to ensure services meet the needs of women and families now and in the future.”

articles.title: Profit warnings from UK-listed firms at highest level in two years as Iran war drives up costs
articles.excerpt:
Consultancy says companies quoted on London stock market issued 65 in three months to end of September

The number of profit warnings from UK-listed companies has risen to the highest level in two yea...
articles.body_text:
Consultancy says companies quoted on London stock market issued 65 in three months to end of September

The number of profit warnings from UK-listed companies has risen to the highest level in two years, as the war in the Middle East triggers a surge in costs for businesses before the budget.

With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s tax and spending statement to the Commons, the consultants EY-Parthenon said companies quoted on the London stock market had issued 65 warnings in the three months to the end of September.

As the war in the Middle East rattles the global economy, business leaders are pressing the chancellor for a package of emergency support to soften the impact from soaring fuel costs and energy bills.

Healey has pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households and businesses “breathing space”. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the conflict pushes the cost of borrowing to the highest level in decades, adding to the pressure on the public finances.

It emerged on Sunday that Healey is preparing to announce measures to help thousands of high street shops, cafes, pubs and hairdressers with rising costs by using the budget to cut business rates for small companies.

In a development that would honour a promise made by Andy Burnham in his Makerfield byelection campaign before entering Downing Street, the planned change, first reported by the Sunday Times, would result in the threshold at which small firms start paying business rates rising from £12,000 to £18,000.

According to the EY-Parthenon analysis, housebuilders have already issued more warnings this year than during the 2008 financial crisis. Separate figures released on Monday from the property platform Rightmove show house prices have fallen by 0.1% over the past 12 months.

Across all listed companies’ profit warnings, the most cited principal factor was policy change and geopolitical uncertainty, with rising costs also playing a large part.

Rising costs were the leading factor for 35% of the warnings issued, while 38% specifically cited the impact of the conflict in the Middle East. Almost a fifth (17%) of all UK-listed businesses have now issued at least one warning over their financial performance in the past 12 months.
 
 
 Jo Robinson of EY-Parthenon said the figures showed how many challenges companies were now navigating: “With the autumn budget around the corner, profit warnings linked to policy change and uncertainty – once concentrated around fiscal events or elections – have become a regular feature of our data.

“Businesses have shown considerable resilience, but the pace of policy change is making forecasting, investment and capital allocation much harder.”

The FTSE sector issuing the most warnings from July to September was household goods and home construction, including six warnings from listed housebuilders, whose 2026 total has reached 14 so far – already past the 10 in 2008, the peak of the global financial crisis.

The property website Rightmove, meanwhile, said average asking prices for newly listed homes had risen by 1% to £371,015 in October. However, over the past year, house prices are down by 0.1%. It also warned that rising mortgage rates were likely to make homes less affordable in a price-sensitive market.

Highlighting the squeeze on households, average two-year fixed mortgage rates have risen to 5.55%, from 5.29% last month, and 4.25% before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. That has added about £250 to average monthly mortgage payments for a new loan.

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: “The rapid rise in mortgage rates is really beginning to hit buyers’ budgets. We’re now seeing mortgage rate rises feed through to seller pricing in many of the cheaper parts of Great Britain, where prices had been more resilient this year.”

Figures from the Trades Union Congress published last week showed UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills over the past five years.

The union umbrella body urged the chancellor to use his budget to launch a cost of living support package funded by higher taxes on wealth and the banking industry.

A scheme to help first-time buyers on to the housing ladder pledged by Burnham is expected to be announced at the budget.

articles.title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
articles.excerpt:
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against women

An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nast...
articles.body_text:
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against women

An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.

Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.

In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.

An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.

Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.

In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.

He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.

Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.

Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.

He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".

Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

A spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader still believed "leave is appropriate under the circumstances" and taking leave would not influence the internal party investigation.

articles.title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
articles.excerpt:
Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island

A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solvin...
articles.body_text:
Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island

A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.

“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.

Previous visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.

The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.

Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.

After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.

By Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.

It said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”

The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.

“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.

The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.

articles.title: Pope greeted by crowds in first major appearance since lung cancer surgery
articles.excerpt:
Pope Leo XIV has thanked some 15,000 Catholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square during his Sunday address, his first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery.

“Now that this delicate ph...
articles.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV has thanked some 15,000 Catholic faithful gathered in St Peter’s Square during his Sunday address, his first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery.

“Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers,” Leo said.

The 71-year-old pontiff addressed the crowd from a window overlooking the square at the Vatican, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing, he revealed that a nodule had been found in his lung and would be surgically removed.

The operation confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.

Leo said the experience of the past week “has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity”.

He told the crowd that he had “truly felt your support” and expressed “particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital” in Rome, where he was treated.

The pope paused for a moment and waved before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.

A delegation from Africa, in Rome for a Catholic meeting, danced and ululated after the pope’s blessing.

“He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo said. “This is an expression of our joy.”

Meanwhile, Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, United States, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.

There had been doubts that a planned papal voyage to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November would go ahead.

The Vatican’s secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told journalists on Friday that the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule “according to the condition of his health”.

But Leo’s surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he believed there were “no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead”.

Latin Americans in the crowd in St Peter’s Square welcomed the news.

“We are all hoping for his recovery, and that he has gotten through the situation well. We know that he is OK, and we’re pleased,” Soledad Espinosa from Ecuador said.

articles.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
articles.excerpt:
Jack Clark, a co-founder and Head of Public Benefit of Anthropic

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public g...
articles.body_text:
Jack Clark, a co-founder and Head of Public Benefit of Anthropic

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn).

The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market.

None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added.

Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday.

Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems

articles.title: Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil’s fiery first presidential run-off debate
articles.excerpt:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro fired off a barrage of personal attacks during their first debate a week before a tight presidential run-off.

In a...
articles.body_text:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro fired off a barrage of personal attacks during their first debate a week before a tight presidential run-off.

In a chaotic exchange on Sunday, the two men called each other “liar” multiple times, accused each other of corruption, dragged up various scandals, and clashed on issues from public security to healthcare.

Lula said Bolsonaro was “a habitual liar” and a “thug”, and physically distanced himself on stage from the candidate he called a “militiaman”, alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary groups.

Bolsonaro, who led the first-round election with 47 percent to Lula’s 45 percent, said it was better to keep Lula at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen”.

Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, paced behind Lula, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing as his adversary spoke.

The 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth term, demanded an explanation regarding a corruption investigation involving the older Bolsonaro, a question his opponent dodged.

The younger Bolsonaro responded by calling Lula a “clown”, and then parried by bringing up a potential corruption case involving one of the president’s sons.

Jair Bolsonaro has been under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 election, which he lost to Lula.

Flavio Bolsonaro hammered away at the top concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and crime, and accused Lula of “reckless spending” to get re-elected, referring to various social measures the president has announced during the campaign.

Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic public spending cuts implemented by Argentina’s right-wing president, Javier Milei.

Bolsonaro dodged the question throughout the debate and pivoted to different topics.

When his father’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic came up, Bolsonaro admitted that this “wasn’t an area where we saw the best results during Bolsonaro’s presidency. I’ll offer a mea culpa here.”

Lula also sought to portray his opponent as out of touch with poor Brazilians, saying Bolsonaro had never used the country’s public healthcare system or taken a bus.

“My opponent only knows about buses from books. He has never even stepped foot on one. He has no idea what the world of work is like,” Lula said.

Ahead of Sunday’s debate, supporters of each candidate gathered en masse in public to show their allegiance.

Pro-Bolsonaro crowds wearing Brazil’s national colours of yellow, green and blue packed Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo’s financial centre, where the candidate addressed the crowd.

Lula supporters wearing red, symbolic of his Workers’ Party, filled Brasilia’s plaza of government buildings, while students backing the president protested against Bolsonaro in Rio de Janeiro.

“We need the current government to remain in power. If another government comes in, we’re, excuse my language, screwed,” said Lula supporter Sonia Maria at the Brasilia rally.

“I don’t like bandits. Out with Lula!” said Bolsonaro backer Vera de Sousa in Sao Paulo.

Also on Sunday, Brazil’s federal police asked the country’s Supreme Court to open an investigation into Bolsonaro over a money laundering accusation involving a lawyer close to him.

The presidential candidate is already under investigation for his links to Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced former banker who financed a movie about Jair Bolsonaro’s life.

Lula spent 580 days in prison in ⁠2018 and 2019 on a corruption conviction that was later annulled over flaws in the investigation and legal proceedings.

Polls suggest a close race for the October 25 run-off, with Flavio Bolsonaro holding a slight advantage after finishing nearly 2 percentage points ahead of Lula in the first round on October 4.

Both candidates hope to engage the 33 million voters who stayed home in the first ⁠round, equal to about one in five eligible voters.

Sunday’s debate was the first between Lula and Bolsonaro after the candidates both ⁠declined previous opportunities. A second debate is scheduled for October 23, just ahead of the run-off.

articles.title: Minns accused of bypassing high court ruling with laws to allow NSW mine to increase coal production by 32%
articles.excerpt:
Bill to authorise production expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, criticised as ‘legislative overreach’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
articles.body_text:
Bill to authorise production expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, criticised as ‘legislative overreach’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Minns government says it will introduce special legislation to allow a mine in the New South Wales Hunter Valley that was the subject of high court proceedings to increase its coal production by 32% per year.

The premier, Chris Minns, said the bill would authorise MACH Energy to increase the annual coal output at its Mount Pleasant coalmine by 4m tonnes to 16.5MT per year until 2032. He claimed it was necessary to save 400 jobs at the site before Christmas.

The move comes less than two weeks after the high court ruled that the approval of an expansion at the mine in Muswellbrook was invalid.

The company is currently permitted to mine up to 12.5MT under a separate modification that was approved in August. That approval extended the mine’s operating life to 2032 and increased the coal extraction rate by 2MT per year.

The government said the legislation would address “unique legal uncertainty arising from the high court’s judgment on 7 October 2026”.

“After discussions with the company, it’s become apparent that there are 400 jobs on the line that will go before Christmas without this intervention,” Minns said on Monday.

He said if the bill passed, MACH Energy had agreed to a “jobs guarantee” to ensure that the current permanent workforce was retained until 2032.

The NSW Greens climate spokesperson and environmental lawyer Sue Higginson said: “This is an incredible new low for the Minns Labor government, bypassing the planning process and the law as laid down by the high court of Australia.

“One thing is clear, under Labor the coal mining giants are writing the laws, and they are laws that will cause significant unassessed climate pollution and hurt communities,” she said.

Georgina Woods, from the Lock the Gate Alliance, accused the government of “cynical and dangerous political interference in the planning system and the courts to increase coal production and coal pollution”.

“Premier Minns is manufacturing a crisis to give special treatment to a coal company – there is no threat to jobs at Mount Pleasant, which already has approval to stay open for another six years,” she said.

“We understand the importance of a safety net for mining communities and back measures that back workers, but this is not about workers. This is about corporate interests trumping the public interest.”

Earlier this month, a majority of the high court found the Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider imposing conditions aimed at minimising emissions generated when the coal was burnt overseas – known as scope 3 emissions – to the greatest extent possible.

Minns said the bill, which will be introduced in the next sitting fortnight, would also include provisions to impose “restrictions” on these emissions that were similar to those in the commission’s recent approval of the state’s largest coal project – the Hunter Valley Operations extension.

“These are not easy decisions. They’re incredibly difficult, and I’ve agonised over this one in particular,” he said.

“But the truth of the matter is, there’s some people who say that the only thing to worry about is industry and jobs in all and every circumstance.

“And there are others who say you should only be worrying about the environment in any and all circumstances. And the truth in our economy and our community is that we have to do both.”

A MACH Energy spokesperson said the company welcomed the announcement, which they said would “deliver operational certainty for the Mount Pleasant mine”.

They claimed the expansion project that was the subject of the company’s unsuccessful high court appeal had been through “a rigorous and exhaustive assessment process over several years”.

“Since that time, the approval has been subject to numerous legal challenges by well-funded activist groups. This has created ongoing fear and uncertainty for local communities who rely on Mount Pleasant for employment, business and community support,” they said.

The director of Johnson Legal, Elaine Johnson, who represented the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg) in the high court proceedings said the government announcement “looks like legislative overreach”.

“The proposed changes to the law to allow an increase in production limits at one mine in NSW makes it look like laws are being written for individual mine owners against the public interest,” she said.

“The mine already has a modified approval allowing continued production until 2032. It’s unclear why it needs legislation to increase its production without going through the proper planning process.

“Communities engaged in good faith in the planning process. This community brought public interest litigation seeking to enforce the law of the land. They won. That decision needs to be respected.”

Asked on Monday if the legislation undermined the high court’s decision, Minns said the government was “not seeking a full approval … just to keep pace with the current workforce and the current profile on the site”.
 
 
 He said Mount Pleasant was the state’s “last legacy mine” and rejected the idea that the legislation set a precedent to secure jobs at other mines.
 
 
 “We don’t have other mines, certainly not at that scale, that are pending a high court decision or an appeal process.”

articles.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
articles.excerpt:
President Emmanuel Macron urged calm in a national address following widespread looting and violence

France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess ...
articles.body_text:
President Emmanuel Macron urged calm in a national address following widespread looting and violence

France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.

On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.

An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.

Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail.

How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account?

How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time?

Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated?

And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education?

Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekend

On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France.

He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests.

The president of France's lower house of parliament, Yaël Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why.

"Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night.

Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines.

That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets.

Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks.

Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets.

What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment.

People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation.

'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight

Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility.

"While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me.

Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order,  posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented".

For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday.

But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests.

Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France

Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

articles.title: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro
articles.excerpt: Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., discusses the indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro on murder and conspiracy charges tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two civilian aircraft that killed four America...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., discusses the indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro on murder and conspiracy charges tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two civilian aircraft that killed four American pilots on ‘Sunday Night in America.’

Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder stemming from the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown, according to a warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose office reopened the state's investigation into Castro after he took office, is expected to announce the new arrest warrant alongside Gov. Ron DeSantis at a press conference Monday morning.The no-bond warrant, issued in Miami-Dade County, directs law enforcement to immediately arrest Castro and says a judge found probable cause to believe he conspired to commit first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of four men aboard the unarmed civilian aircraft.The warrant marks a new front in efforts to hold Castro accountable for the Feb. 24, 1996, attack, which has long reverberated through South Florida's Cuban-American community. Castro already faces a separate federal prosecution over the shootdown.

HAVANA REGIME IN SUSPENSE AFTER CASTRO INDICTMENT WITH TRUMP PRESSURE ON, SAYS CUBAN-BORN GOP REP.

Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. (AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa)

"The investigation revealed evidence of a conspiracy to kill persons aboard BTTR aircraft. The deaths of Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr. were the object of that conspiracy," the warrant reads.

According to the warrant, investigators allege that in 1996, the Castro regime's foreign intelligence service's plan to shoot down Brothers to the Rescue aircraft and kill their occupants traveled through the chain of command, with Raúl Castro and his brother, former Cuban leader Fidel Castro, as the final decision-makers.

Raúl and Fidel Castro attend a parade Dec. 2, 1996, in Havana, Cuba. (Sven Creutzmann/Mambo Photography/Getty Images)

"They have violated the airspace, the waters of the Republic. I made it clear that this had to be decentralized if we wanted it to do its job, and five generals were given the authority. I used to say: Try to shoot them down over our territory. But they would come into Havana and leave," Raúl Castro, now 95, said in a recorded statement months after the incident, recounting orders he gave to senior military leaders before the shootdown, according to the warrant.

"Of course, with a missile shot like that, plane against plane, what comes down is a ball of fire, and it is going to fall on top of the city. So I said: Fine, shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone," he added in his statement.

RAÚL CASTRO MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CHARGED HIM WITH MURDER

The attorney general’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Raúl Castro. (Joe Burbank/Orlando Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Brothers to the Rescue is a Miami-based organization that flew unarmed civilian aircraft to search for Cuban migrants stranded or lost at sea. By the mid-1990s, the group had also become involved in anti-Castro political activity, including dropping pro-democracy leaflets over Cuba.

The Cuban government has rejected the U.S. prosecution of Castro, maintaining that Brothers to the Rescue repeatedly violated Cuban airspace and that Cuba acted in defense of its sovereignty.

The warrant indicates that Florida authorities are seeking full extradition of Raúl Castro if he is arrested outside the Sunshine State, authorizing authorities to pursue his return to Florida to face the felony charge if he is arrested in another U.S. jurisdiction.

The attorney general’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Castro.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia on edge: Iconic Kingdom Centre sends workers home amid Houthi attacks
articles.excerpt:
Gen. Jack Keane (Ret.) and Jeff Smith provide analysis on Houthi rebels escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia as China is suspected of offering help.

One of Saudi Arabia’s most iconic skyscrapers ordere...
articles.body_text:
Gen. Jack Keane (Ret.) and Jeff Smith provide analysis on Houthi rebels escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia as China is suspected of offering help.

One of Saudi Arabia’s most iconic skyscrapers ordered office workers to stay home Sunday as escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels rattled the capital of Riyadh amid fears of a widening Middle East conflict.

The move came after the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area, a third over the Eastern Province and two ballistic missiles in southern Saudi Arabia overnight, after authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital, also shared on X.

Management at the 99-story Kingdom Centre, a landmark on Riyadh's skyline, ordered office employees to work remotely until further notice, according to reporting by Agence France-Presse (AFP).

The directive affects a building whose tenants include major international financial institutions such as Merrill Lynch, consulting giant McKinsey & Company and the International Monetary Fund.

THE HOUTHIS AREN'T SOMEBODY ELSE'S PROBLEM. AMERICA CAN'T AFFORD TO LOOK AWAY

One of Saudi Arabia's most iconic skyscrapers ordered office workers to stay home as escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels rattled the capital of Riyadh amid fears of a widening Middle East conflict.  (Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Please be advised that remote working arrangements are mandatory for all office employees at Kingdom Centre, effective immediately and until further notice," building management said in an email obtained by AFP.

Employees were instructed not to report back to their offices. The shopping mall at the base of the tower, however, remained open to the public.

Management did not specify a reason for the directive, but it came as repeated missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Houthis disrupted the Saudi capital.

The security concerns also follow a deadly Oct. 10 attack on King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, another strike the following day killed one person and injured 11.

Airport operations have been severely disrupted, while schools in Riyadh have extended remote learning measures amid continued security threats.

SAUDI ARABIA FACING 'BIGGEST THREAT' EVER TO OIL PRODUCTION AS IRAN-PROXY HOUTHIS LAUNCH ATTACKS, EXPERT SAYS

The Houthis also attacked Abha International Airport in Saudi Arabia. (AFPTV / AFP via Getty Images)

The mounting crisis comes as Saudi Arabia's military reported two deaths in a helicopter crash near its southern border with Yemen.

Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said Sunday that an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter crashed in the Najran region because of a technical malfunction, killing both crew members.

Saudi civil defense authorities also reported Sunday that six people were injured when a hostile projectile struck a residential neighborhood in Najran, damaging three homes and three vehicles.

Meanwhile, Egypt moved toward potentially providing military assistance to Saudi Arabia as the kingdom confronts the growing Houthi threat.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi requested an emergency parliamentary session to authorize defensive military support for Saudi Arabia if requested by Riyadh, Reuters reported.

Lawmakers were expected to continue discussions Monday.

NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

A Houthi follower looks on, during a pro-Iran demonstration, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues, in Sanaa, Yemen April 6, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)

The Egyptian presidency said Cairo was prepared to provide Saudi Arabia with necessary support to defend its security, stability, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites.

The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defense Council chaired by el-Sissi and attended by senior government and military officials.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan about regional developments and the importance of de-escalation, according to a post on X.

The potential involvement of Egypt, which has one of the Arab world's largest militaries, could significantly expand the regional response to the Houthis.

The Iran-backed group now controls Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north.

Fighting with the Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen's internationally recognized government, has intensified amid the broader U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Tampa Bay Rays move one win from World Series after Drew Rasmussen dominates Cleveland Guardians

The Tampa Bay Rays sit just one win away from the World Series after putting on a postseason clinic in Cleveland on Sunday.

Behind a pitching gem from Drew Rasmussen, Tampa Bay silenced Progressive F...
articles.body_text:
The Tampa Bay Rays sit just one win away from the World Series after putting on a postseason clinic in Cleveland on Sunday.

Behind a pitching gem from Drew Rasmussen, Tampa Bay silenced Progressive Field with a clinical 3-1 Game 5 victory, seizing a 3-2 series lead that pushes the Guardians to the brink of elimination and sets up a potential World Series showdown against Milwaukee.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Jose Ramirez of the Cleveland Guardians celebrates a single during the sixth inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series at Progressive Field on Oct. 18, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Getty Images)

Drew Rasmussen of the Tampa Bay Rays reacts to a double play during the seventh inning against the Cleveland Guardians in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series at Progressive Field on Oct. 18, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Getty Images)

Rasmussen was lights-out. Over seven strong innings, he surrendered just one run on four hits and gave Cleveland virtually no room to breathe. The Guardians had no answers at the plate, and when they threatened again in the seventh, Rasmussen erased the danger with a 6-4-3 double play.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Rays didn't need big home runs to take control; they simply chipped away early. Jonny DeLuca worked a bases-loaded walk in the first, Jonathan Aranda lined an RBI single in the second, and Liam Hicks dropped in an RBI single of his own in the third.

Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays celebrates with assistant hitting coach Ozzie Timmons in the dugout before Game 5 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field on Oct. 18, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Cleveland looked flat from start to finish. The Guardians had no rhythm at the plate, swinging right through Rasmussen's best pitches and struggling to string at-bats together. Their only run came on an infield groundout in the sixth, and Tampa Bay's bullpen locked down the final six outs without breaking a sweat, capped by Bryan Baker closing it out in the ninth.

BREWERS MANAGER HAS EPIC QUOTE STRAIGHT FROM HOLLYWOOD SCRIPT AFTER SWEEPING VAUNTED DODGERS

The series now heads back south to St. Petersburg for Game 6. The Rays have two chances on their home turf to capture the American League pennant, while the Guardians have to find a way to revive their offense.

Junior Caminero #13 of the Tampa Bay Rays leaves the field during Game 5 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (MLB Photos via Getty Images)

articles.title: Ohio State QB Julian Sayin's injury may completely reshape the College Football Playoff race
articles.excerpt:
Ryan Day and Jeremiah Smith spoke to Jenny Taft and Tom Rinaldi after the Ohio State Buckeyes' 19-15 over the Indiana Hoosiers.

It was a stunning week seven in the world of college football, both for...
articles.body_text:
Ryan Day and Jeremiah Smith spoke to Jenny Taft and Tom Rinaldi after the Ohio State Buckeyes' 19-15 over the Indiana Hoosiers.

It was a stunning week seven in the world of college football, both for the number of top programs that lost, and for who they lost to.

BYU took down Notre Dame, with a little help from yet another controversial last-second game clock issue. Auburn beat the heavily favored Georgia Bulldogs in Athens. Florida rose from the dead to upset Texas in Austin on the back of another disappointing performance from Arch Manning. Tennessee had a big home win over Alabama, holding the powerful Crimson Tide offense to just 10 points. Miami held on to beat Florida State thanks to some questionable officiating, but just not losing bumped the Hurricanes up to No. 1.

But arguably the most impactful win of the weekend was The Ohio State Buckeyes ending Indiana's 22-game winning streak in Bloomington. With around a minute remaining, Indiana seemed to tie it when Josh Hoover hit a wide open Nick Marsh in the end zone. Marsh's foot came down just out of bounds, however, and Ohio State hung on to the 19-15 win.

WEEK 7 AP TOP 25 POLL FEATURES A COMPLETE SHUFFLE AFTER CHAOTIC WEEKEND, WITH MIAMI TAKING OVER THE TOP SPOT

Julian Sayin #10 of the Ohio State Buckeyes looks to throw over Tobi Osunsanmi #12 of the Indiana Hoosiers during the second quarter at Memorial Stadium on Oct. 17, 2026, in Bloomington, Ind. (Getty Images)

Thanks to the 12-team playoff, the win for OSU and loss for Indiana wouldn't typically mean either team is out of the running. And this week's AP Top 25 Poll reflects that; Ohio State is No. 3, and Indiana is No. 5, thanks to the carnage around them.

So how could it be the most impactful? Because of what happened to starting quarterback Julian Sayin's shoulder in the fourth quarter.

Indiana defensive lineman Mario Landino sacked Sayin in the fourth quarter, forcing a fumble and the injury when he hit the ground. The 21-year-old junior immediately could be seen favoring his right arm and went to the locker room, emerging a few minutes afterward with his arm in a sling.

After the game, head coach Ryan Day was light on specifics, saying he didn't have further details on what exactly the injury was, but did admit that Sayin's likely to miss "several weeks."

Day was adamant that true freshman backup Luke Fahey would be able to step in, particularly with a bye week approaching.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Julian Sayin of the Ohio State Buckeyes walks off the field with his arm in a sling after defeating the Indiana Hoosiers at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind., on Oct. 17, 2026. (Getty Images)

"We'll regroup," he said. "We've got a good team. When Luke's in there, we just may need to do things just a little bit differently, but the bye week gives us a chance to regroup on that and put our heads together."

After replacing Sayin, Fahey went 0-2 passing, though he did draw a penalty that helped extend a Buckeyes' drive. The bye week reps will help, but as a true freshman, Fahey's light on college experience and now thrust into the starting role at a pivotal time. Which is why Sayin's injury could reshape the playoff picture.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Though OSU has the bye week coming up, their next game is on the road against the No. 16 USC Trojans. With Sayin, the Buckeyes would be sizable favorites. With a true freshman backup? The calculus might change significantly. The SC defense isn't Indiana, but making your first career start, on the road, in front of what's sure to be a sold-out, hostile LA Coliseum crowd, against a team hungry to make statement and reach the College Football Playoff for the first time in Lincoln Riley's tenure? It's not ideal, to say the least.

If Sayin isn't able to return after SC, the Buckeyes return home to face ... Oregon. While that matchup no longer looks like the battle of top-5 teams it looked like in the preseason, the Ducks' defense is still extremely talented, and even with their backup QB's, pulled out an impressive win against a very good Nebraska team.

The schedule doesn't get much easier after that either. Ranked Northwestern comes to Columbus. Then the Buckeyes travel to Lincoln to play Nebraska, and host Michigan in "The Game."

Without further specifics on Sayin's injury, it's hard to say how many games he might miss, but even the SC game alone could have enormous ramifications. USC is on the playoff bubble, but if the Trojans beat Wisconsin and OSU, now with Fahey playing, they'd immediately move into the top-10. A slip up at home against a still dangerous Oregon team, and the Buckeyes could suddenly be on the outside of the top-12 looking in.
